classification.difficultyReason: Choose the smaller group in unequal-size cases and apply the preceding question's double-counting correction to equal groups.

content.prompt: In how many ways can a group of six people be divided into:

children.label: a
children.prompt: two unequal groups (neither group being empty),

answer.worked:
The possible group sizes are $(1,5)$ and $(2,4)$. Choose the smaller group in each case; the remaining people form the other group.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of splits}&={}^{6}C_{1}+{}^{6}C_{2}\\&=6+15\\&=21.\end{aligned}$$

Choose three people for one group. Each split is counted twice because the groups are indistinguishable.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of splits}&=\frac{{}^{6}C_{3}}{2}\\&=\frac{20}{2}\\&=10.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: c
children.prompt: Repeat part a for four people.

answer.worked:
The only unequal non-empty group sizes are $(1,3)$. Choose the person in the smaller group:
$$\text{Number of splits}={}^{4}C_{1}=4.$$

children.label: d
children.prompt: Repeat part b for four people.

answer.worked:
Choose two people, then divide by two because swapping the groups gives the same split.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of splits}&=\frac{{}^{4}C_{2}}{2}\\&=\frac{6}{2}\\&=3.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: e
children.prompt: Repeat part a for eight people.

answer.worked:
The possible sizes are $(1,7)$, $(2,6)$ and $(3,5)$. Choose the smaller group in each case.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of splits}&={}^{8}C_{1}+{}^{8}C_{2}+{}^{8}C_{3}\\&=8+28+56\\&=92.\end{aligned}$$

children.label: f
children.prompt: Repeat part b for eight people.

answer.worked:
Choose four people, then divide by two because swapping the groups gives the same split.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Number of splits}&=\frac{{}^{8}C_{4}}{2}\\&=\frac{70}{2}\\&=35.\end{aligned}$$
